title: UK's Skilled Worker Visa Under Fire as Kebab Shops and Gurdwaras Outnumber Engineers on Sponsor List
excerpt: Home Office data reveals 159 kebab shops, dozens of mosques and gurdwaras hold licences to sponsor overseas workers, raising questions about whether Britain's immigration system serves its stated purpose.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • 159 kebab shops hold skilled worker visa licences, alongside various community organizations.
  • Critics argue the visa scheme has strayed from filling skilled vacancies in key sectors.
  • New salary threshold of £38,700 raises cost pressures for food and hospitality sectors.
  • Community institutions rely on specific skilled workers, risking cultural infrastructure if visa access is lost.

A Sponsorship System Under Scrutiny

Britain's Skilled Worker Visa programme was sold to the public as a mechanism for filling critical vacancies in sectors where domestic talent falls short — engineering, healthcare, scientific research. But Home Office sponsorship data tells a different story.

According to the latest figures, 159 kebab shops now hold licences to sponsor overseas workers through the scheme. They are joined by car washes, vape retailers, fish and chip shops, and — more notably for the South Asian diaspora — dozens of mosques, gurdwaras, and community religious organisations.

The revelation has reignited a fierce debate about the direction of Britain's immigration policy and whether the system designed for high-skilled recruitment has quietly expanded to cover roles that were traditionally filled from the domestic workforce.

Religious Institutions and Community Organisations

Among the more striking entries on the sponsor register are Sikh gurdwaras and Islamic mosques that have obtained licences to bring in religious workers, community organisers, and support staff from abroad. While these roles serve genuine community needs — particularly in areas with large South Asian and Muslim populations — their presence on a "skilled worker" register has drawn criticism from those who argue the scheme lacks coherent boundaries.

The food sector's presence on the list is even more pronounced. Between the first quarter of 2022 and mid-2023, visas were granted to around 2,500 butchers, over 400 fishmongers and poultry dressers, and more than 6,000 chefs across retail, wholesale, and manufacturing, according to analysis by law firm Eversheds Sutherland.

"A nation once obsessed with building things now seems obsessed with administering schemes. The result is a country where the definition of 'skilled worker' appears to be expanding faster than the economy itself."

— Gary Thomas, immigration policy commentator

Salary Threshold Creates New Pressures

The UK government's spring 2024 immigration reforms raised the minimum salary for sponsored overseas workers from around £26,200 to £38,700 — a 48 percent increase designed to encourage domestic hiring and reduce net migration.

But the British Meat Processors Association warned that meat producers operating on 2 percent margins cannot absorb such costs. The trade body estimated the increase "could cost hundreds of millions of pounds" for the meat processing sector alone, with higher expenses inevitably passed on to consumers through food price inflation.

For employers in regions outside London and the South East, where prevailing wages are lower, the new threshold effectively prices out many roles that were previously eligible — creating what the Association of Labour Providers called a "disproportionate impact" on food businesses.

The Diaspora Dimension

For Britain's Indian diaspora, the debate cuts both ways. Community institutions like gurdwaras rely on specialist religious workers — granthis, ragis, and sevadars — whose skills are highly specific but may not command the salary levels now required under the scheme. Losing access to the visa route could affect the cultural and spiritual infrastructure that serves an estimated 500,000 British Sikhs.

At the same time, many in the diaspora community are among those who argue that the skilled worker route should prioritise genuinely high-skilled roles. Indian-origin professionals in technology, finance, and healthcare have long navigated the system and question whether its credibility is undermined by the breadth of sponsors now on the register.

What Comes Next

A National Audit Office inquiry into the scheme's effectiveness is underway, examining whether the Home Office has adequate oversight of sponsor licences and whether the "genuine vacancy test" is being meaningfully applied. The inquiry has heard evidence of exploitation in some sponsored roles, particularly in the care sector, where the power imbalance inherent in visa sponsorship creates vulnerability.

Research from the Centre for Global Development suggests that for many roles, losing visa access would create a "significant supply shock" that domestic training pipelines cannot quickly replace — particularly given weak apprenticeship completion rates and long training lead times.

The question facing policymakers is not whether kebab shops should employ workers, but whether a system designed for one purpose has quietly become something else entirely — and whether the communities that depend on it, from Southall gurdwaras to Midlands meat processors, will bear the cost of reform.
